title: Music
subtitle: tracks, playlists, play by ear
summary: Talk about the music you listen to and the way you listen to it - tracks and playlists, the people in a band, kinds of music, and the collocations musicians use.

lesson.heading: Downloading and managing your music
lesson.text: Downloading music as **MP3** files is easy. An MP3 is a popular type of audio file that you can listen to on a computer or mobile device.

examples.text: You can download a whole **album** or individual **tracks** onto your phone or computer.
examples.note: a track = one song or piece of music from an album

examples.text: You can save your favourite albums and tracks in **playlists** so you can find them easily.
You can **sync** the music files on your computer with your phone.
examples.note: sync (more formal: synchronise) = have exactly the same files and data on more than one device

examples.text: You can also **stream** music from the Internet to other rooms in your home.
examples.note: stream = play music in real time from one source to another

lesson.heading: A typical rock band
rows: the lead singer - sings the songs
the lead guitarist - plays the highest notes on the guitar
the bass guitarist, or just *the bass* - plays the lowest notes
the keyboard player - plays an electric piano or organ
the drummer - keeps the rhythm with two sticks
lesson.note: If it is obvious you are talking about a band, you can say *the bass* rather than *the bass player*.

lesson.heading: Talking about the band
lesson.text: Notice that we say someone **plays** an instrument, and that many band roles have both a noun for the instrument and a noun for the person.

examples.text: She's **lead singer** in a rock band. One of her brothers plays **lead guitar** and her other brother is a **keyboard player**, so it's a real family band.
What would you rather play in a band, **drums** or **bass**?
I could never be a **drummer** but I think I could become a fairly good **bass guitarist**.

lesson.heading: Types of music
lesson.text: One family, many different tastes. If you are **into** a kind of music, you are interested in it and enthusiastic about it.

examples.text: My sister Niki loves **classical music**, my uncle Ben's a **folk** fan and my father loves **jazz**.
I like **R&B** and **hip-hop**. I even compose a bit of **rap** myself!
examples.note: R&B = Rhythm and Blues, originally a black American form of blues with a strong rhythm; hip-hop = a style of popular music where the words are spoken rather than sung; rap = the words spoken in hip-hop

examples.text: My older brother is **into** The Beatles and other **60s music**.
My mother loves film **soundtracks** but I just find them uninteresting.
examples.note: a soundtrack = the music from a film or TV show

examples.text: One type of music I can't stand is the **canned music** you get in supermarkets and airports.
examples.note: canned music = artificial or recorded music played in the background

lesson.heading: Collocations for musical activities
lesson.text: These phrases come up whenever people talk about musical ability. *A good ear* and *pick out* are informal.

examples.text: She plays the guitar but she doesn't **read music**. She plays **by ear**.
She's got a **good ear**. She can **pick out** a tune on almost any instrument.
You can **make music** in lots of ways. You don't need to be a **trained musician** to enjoy music **to the full**.

lesson.text: Say **classical music**, never ~~classic music~~ - and remember that *music* is uncountable, so *they played fantastic music*, not ~~fantastic musics~~.

exercises.prompt: In a typical rock band, who does what?

pairs.left: keeps the rhythm using two sticks
plays an electric piano or organ
plays the highest notes on the guitar

exercises.prompt: I downloaded the songs to a ___ on my phone, so I can find them easily.
exercises.explanation: You save favourite albums and tracks in playlists.

exercises.prompt: I just got six ___ from the new album, not the whole thing.
exercises.explanation: A track is one song or piece of music from an album.

exercises.prompt: I download music files but then forget to ___ them with my phone, so I don't have them when I travel.
exercises.explanation: To sync (formally, synchronise) is to have exactly the same files on more than one device.

exercises.prompt: I can ___ music from the computer in my study to the audio system in the living room.
exercises.hint: (play it in real time from one source to another)
exercises.explanation: You stream music when it plays in real time from one source to another.

exercises.prompt: Six people describe what they listen to. Match each comment with the kind of music.

pairs.left: I love the film and I'm going to buy the music from it.
I just love the way they can speak the words so fast.
I love the old original tracks by The Beatles and the Rolling Stones.
I listen to the traditional songs of my country.
I've always loved the blues and I like music with a strong rhythm.
I must be the only person who actually likes the music in supermarkets.

exercises.prompt: Do you have a good ___ for music?
exercises.explanation: To have a good ear is to be able to hear and reproduce music accurately.

exercises.prompt: She never looks at the printed notes - she plays entirely ___ ear.
exercises.explanation: To play by ear is to play from memory or by listening, not from written music.

exercises.prompt: Can you ___ out a tune on an instrument you've never played before?
exercises.explanation: To pick out a tune is to work it out and play it, often slowly, without music.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order to complete the advertisement.
exercises.answer: You don't need to be a trained musician to enjoy music to the full.
exercises.explanation: A trained musician is someone who has studied music formally; *to the full* means completely.

exercises.prompt: Is each word a kind of music or a person in a band?

exercises.explanation: We say *classical music*, never *classic music*, and *music* is uncountable.

exercises.statement: They played fantastic musics for an hour.
exercises.explanation: *Music* is uncountable: They played fantastic music for an hour.
